propositions.text: The Appellant is a Pakistani citizen appealing the RPD's denial of refugee protection.
The Appellant has not submitted new evidence or requested an oral hearing.
The Appellant requests the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and allow his claim.
Alternatively, the Appellant requests the RAD to remit the matter to the RPD for reconsideration by a different panel.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant, a Pakistani citizen, appeals the RPD's denial without new evidence or oral hearing, requesting the RAD to allow the claim or remit for reconsideration.

propositions.text: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of IRPA, the RAD confirms the RPD decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
The appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision denying refugee status and dismisses the appeal, pursuant to IRPA section 111(1)(a).

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges he is a Shia Muslim active in his religious community.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges he is a Shia Muslim active in his religious community.

propositions.text: The Appellant left Pakistan in 2009 fearing life risk from brothers over father's estate conflict.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant left Pakistan in 2009 fearing threats from his brothers over estate conflict.

propositions.text: He travelled to the UK on a study visa in 2009 and attended school until 2011 when it closed.
His study visa expired in 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant studied in the UK from 2009 to 2011; his study visa expired in 2012.

propositions.text: He returned to Pakistan in 2011 for about 1.5 months and resolved problems with his brothers.

paragraphs.summary: He returned to Pakistan in 2011 briefly and resolved issues with his brothers.

propositions.text: He made an unsuccessful refugee claim in the UK in 2012 and was deported to Pakistan in 2014.

paragraphs.summary: He unsuccessfully claimed refugee status in the UK in 2012 and was deported in 2014.

propositions.text: In Pakistan, he resumed supporting the local Imam and started receiving threatening calls in 2014.

paragraphs.summary: In 2014, back in Pakistan, he resumed religious support and received threats.

propositions.text: He was assaulted in 2014 and threatened to be killed if he continued community activities; threats extended to family after coming to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: He was assaulted and threatened in 2014; threats continued to family after arriving in Canada.

propositions.text: He fears the threatening group and states police protection and internal flight alternative are unavailable.

paragraphs.summary: He fears the threatening group and says police protection and internal flight alternative are unavailable.

propositions.text: The RPD panel found credibility to be the determinative issue in the claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD panel found credibility to be the key issue in the claim.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the issues are the appropriate standard of review and whether the RPD erred in credibility findings including documentary evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the issues are the standard of review and errors in RPD credibility findings.

propositions.text: IRPA sets out grounds for appeal and remedies but does not specify the RAD's standard of review.

paragraphs.summary: IRPA provides appeal grounds and remedies but not the RAD's standard of review.

propositions.text: The RAD benefits from Federal Court jurisprudence on its appellate role relative to the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD relies on Federal Court jurisprudence about its appellate role relative to the RPD.

propositions.text: Huruglica case determined the RAD conducts a hybrid appeal, reviewing all aspects and independently assessing claims, deferring to RPD only where it has advantage.

paragraphs.summary: Huruglica holds the RAD conducts a hybrid appeal, independently assessing claims but deferring to RPD's advantage.

propositions.text: RAD can respect RPD credibility conclusions but is not restricted to intervening only on palpable and overriding error.

paragraphs.summary: RAD may respect RPD credibility findings but is not limited to intervening only for palpable and overriding error.

propositions.text: The RAD reviews all RPD evidence and independently assesses refugee or protection status.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD reviews all evidence and independently assesses refugee or protection status.

propositions.text: The RAD notes the Appellant's brief analysis aligns with the RAD's stated view on standard of review.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the Appellant's analysis aligns with the RAD's view on standard of review.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant stated risk in Pakistan due to religious activities and questioned his UK religious activities from 2009-2014.
The Appellant said he attended mosque for Friday prayers whenever possible, about four times a month.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the Appellant's stated risk from religious activities and questioned his UK mosque attendance, which he said was about four times monthly.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant testified he intended to serve his religious community in the UK but was unable to spare time.
He was deported in 2014 and thought his UK problems resulted from lack of religious service.
He testified he attended the majlis only once every two months.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the Appellant's testimony of limited religious service in the UK, attributing problems to this, and infrequent majlis attendance.

propositions.text: The panel asked the Appellant for corroborating evidence of UK religious observance such as a letter, photograph or receipt.
The Appellant responded he did not do anything in the UK and donations were made by his wife in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The panel asked the Appellant for corroborating evidence of UK religious observance; the Appellant said he did nothing there and his wife made donations in Pakistan.

propositions.text: The panel drew a negative inference about the Appellant's credibility due to lack of UK religious involvement inconsistent with alleged Pakistan activities.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the Appellant's lack of UK religious involvement inconsistent with his Pakistan activities and drew a negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits lack of UK religious activity does not discredit his religious activism in Pakistan.
He explained difficulty finding time for community service while working and studying in the UK.
His testimony was consistent with his Basis of Claim narrative.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues his lack of UK religious activity does not discredit his Pakistan activism, citing time constraints and consistent testimony.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's finding that his UK religious testimony evolved was unsubstantiated and unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the panel's finding that his UK religious testimony evolved was unsubstantiated and unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's requirement for objective corroboration of his low UK religious involvement was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the panel's demand for objective corroboration of his low UK religious involvement was unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's negative credibility inference about his UK Shia community lack of involvement is unreasonable given the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits the panel's negative credibility inference about his UK Shia involvement is unreasonable given the circumstances.

propositions.text: The RAD reviewed all evidence about the Appellant's UK religious activities and found no specific panel findings on lack of corroboration or evolving testimony.
The RAD finds the Appellant's lack of substantive UK religious activity for 4.5 years raises doubt about his commitment to Shia Islam and concurs with the panel's finding.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD reviewed evidence and concurs with the panel that the Appellant's lack of UK religious activity raises doubt about his Shia Islam commitment.

propositions.text: The panel noted a UK Home Office document suggesting false documents were submitted to extend the Appellant's study visa.
The Appellant explained a lawyer attached false documents without his knowledge and he took no responsibility.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted UK documents suggesting false visa extension documents; the Appellant said a lawyer attached them without his knowledge.

propositions.text: The panel found the Appellant was the only beneficiary of the false documents and did not believe he was unaware of their use.
The panel drew a negative inference about the Appellant's credibility regarding the false documents.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the Appellant benefited from false documents and did not believe he was unaware, drawing a negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's finding about false documents is unreasonable due to his dependence on a lawyer and irrelevance to his Canadian claim.
He submits the misrepresentations do not determine credibility of material incidents in Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the panel's finding on false documents is unreasonable and irrelevant to his Canadian claim's credibility.

propositions.text: The RAD finds UK incidents do not go to the core of the Canadian refugee claim but raise doubt about the Appellant's general credibility.
The RAD finds the Appellant's claim of unawareness about fraudulent documents strains credulity given his visa application knowledge.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds UK incidents raise doubt about the Appellant's credibility and his unawareness claim strains credulity.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant filed a UK form indicating he was single without children, which was false.
The Appellant explained a consultant advised him to lie to avoid visa denial due to past refusals and danger.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the Appellant falsely indicated single status on a UK form; the Appellant explained consultant advice to avoid visa denial.

propositions.text: The panel found the Appellant willing to say whatever suited him to immigration authorities.
The panel noted the Appellant's UK lawyer said he was a torture victim; the Appellant was unsure what this referred to but later said he was beaten by brothers in 2011.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the Appellant willing to say whatever suited him; noted lawyer's torture claim and Appellant's later admission of 2011 beating.

propositions.text: The panel noted no mention of torture in the Basis of Claim Form and drew a negative inference from inconsistent information.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted no torture mention in the Basis of Claim Form and drew a negative inference from inconsistent information.

propositions.text: The Appellant said he told counsel's interpreter about beatings and detention and forgot to include them in the BOC due to stress.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant said he told counsel's interpreter about beatings and detention but forgot to include them in the BOC due to stress.

propositions.text: The panel drew a negative inference from omissions due to lack of medical documentation explaining forgetfulness.

paragraphs.summary: The panel drew a negative inference from omissions due to no medical documentation explaining forgetfulness.

propositions.text: The RAD notes the Appellant makes no submission regarding the negative inference from omissions.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the Appellant makes no submission regarding the negative inference from omissions.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant's study visa expired in 2012, possibly 2011 when school closed, and he remained illegally working until arrest and refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the Appellant overstayed his visa, worked illegally until arrest, then made a refugee claim in 2012.

propositions.text: The panel noted the Appellant claimed protection only after arrest and his illegal stay negatively impacts credibility and shows lack of subjective fear.

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the Appellant's claim after arrest and illegal stay negatively impacts credibility and shows lack of subjective fear.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the panel's finding about overstay does not reasonably lead to adverse credibility findings about persecution incidents in Pakistan.
He submits overstay does not lead to lack of subjective fear about persecution incidents.
He notes the panel failed to distinguish incidents prompting UK stay from those prompting Canada claim.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the panel's overstay finding does not justify adverse credibility or lack of fear findings and failed to distinguish UK and Canada claim incidents.

propositions.text: RAD agrees Appellant's UK overstay does not affect credibility of persecution claim evidence
Appellant's UK actions raise doubt about his general credibility
Letters from Imam XXXX are relevant

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellant's UK overstay does not affect persecution claim credibility but raises general credibility doubts; letters from Imam XXXX are relevant.

propositions.text: Appellant corroborated fear with 2015 letter from Imam XXXX president about threats due to Shia conversion
Appellant claimed to be Shia from birth, persecution agent is XXXX not XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX
Appellant had brother seek replacement letter after inconsistencies, mailed in 2015
Letter writer said he wrote letter for someone else but sent it to Appellant by mistake

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the Appellant's fear corroborated by a 2015 letter with inconsistencies; Appellant claimed Shia from birth and replacement letter was sought; letter writer said letter was for someone else.

propositions.text: Second letter explained errors as 'a typo mistake on my part'

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the second letter explained errors as a typographical mistake by the letter writer.

propositions.text: Initial letter accurate in many respects including Appellant's name and role in Imam XXXX
Appellant explained initial letter noted conversion to Shia Islam as written for someone else
Appellant did not know why agent of persecution mistake was made; letter writer said it was a mistake
Appellant said letter writer said mistake happened to someone else and he cut and pasted

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the initial letter was accurate; Appellant explained conversion note as letter for someone else; he did not know agent mistake reason; letter writer said it was a cut and paste error.

propositions.text: Appellant explained discrepancies as letter written for someone else
Second letter said discrepancies were 'a typo mistake on my part' not matching Appellant's explanation

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted Appellant's explanation of discrepancies differs from second letter's claim of typographical error.

propositions.text: Appellant's explanations evolved and no reason given why initial letter was accurate in many parts
Typographical error explanation not persuasive for conversion and agent of persecution issues

paragraphs.summary: The panel found Appellant's evolving explanations unconvincing and typographical error explanation not persuasive on key issues.

propositions.text: Two letters are completely unreliable and possibly fraudulent
Letters accorded no weight
Negative inference drawn on Appellant's credibility due to letters

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the two letters unreliable, possibly fraudulent, accorded no weight, and drew negative credibility inference against Appellant.

propositions.text: Panel's negative credibility inference is unreasonable
Letter writer provided reasonable explanation for errors
Panel's phrase cited is ambiguous or unintelligible, casting doubt on findings

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the panel's negative credibility inference is unreasonable, letter writer's explanation reasonable, and panel's phrase ambiguous.

propositions.text: RAD reviewed evidence and is not persuaded letter writer's explanation is reasonable
RAD finds panel did not err on letters and explanations
RAD agrees with panel's analysis on letters and explanations

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds letter writer's explanation unreasonable, no error by panel, and agrees with panel's analysis on letters.

propositions.text: RAD agrees panel's phrase is ambiguous and reflects poor proofreading
Ambiguous phrase does not cast doubt on reliability of panel's findings

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees the panel's phrase is ambiguous due to poor proofreading but it does not affect reliability of findings.

propositions.text: Appellant provided medical report dated 2014 about injuries from beating

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted the Appellant provided a 2014 medical report about injuries from a beating.

propositions.text: Appellant testified mother got doctor to misrepresent medical document to restore peace
Appellant acknowledged mother's medical document was fraudulent
Panel noted ease of obtaining fraudulent documents in Pakistan
Appellant did not explain why his medical document should be considered authentic

paragraphs.summary: The panel noted Appellant admitted mother's medical document was fraudulent and ease of fraud in Pakistan; Appellant did not explain authenticity of his own document.

propositions.text: Ease of obtaining fraudulent documents in Pakistan does not render Appellant's medical report inauthentic
Mother's fraudulent document does not indicate Appellant's document is fraudulent

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues ease of fraud in Pakistan and mother's fraudulent document do not mean his medical report is fraudulent.

propositions.text: Panel failed to make definitive finding on authenticity of Appellant's medical report, a reviewable error

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits the panel erred by not definitively finding on authenticity of his medical report.

propositions.text: RAD agrees ease of fraud and mother's fraudulent document do not necessarily mean Appellant's document is fraudulent
RAD agrees panel did not make definitive finding on authenticity of Appellant's medical document

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees ease of fraud and mother's document do not prove Appellant's document fraudulent and panel made no definitive finding on authenticity.

propositions.text: Medical document lists injuries but no evidence on perpetrators or reasons for assault
RAD gives medical document little evidentiary weight on central issue

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the medical document lists injuries but lacks evidence on perpetrators or reasons and gives it little weight.

propositions.text: Panel found Appellant not credible witness
Panel found Appellant's allegations of attack, threats, and risks in Pakistan not true
Panel concluded Appellant did not provide sufficient credible evidence for positive claim determination

paragraphs.summary: The panel found the Appellant not credible, his allegations untrue, and concluded insufficient credible evidence for claim success.

propositions.text: Panel did not provide valid reasons for rebutting presumption of truthfulness

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submits the panel failed to provide valid reasons for rebutting his presumption of truthfulness.

propositions.text: RAD finds Appellant's untruthfulness and delay in UK claim raise doubt on general credibility
Disclosure of likely fraudulent letters and explanation discrepancies rebut presumption of truthfulness

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant's untruthfulness, delay, and likely fraudulent letters rebut presumption of truthfulness.

propositions.text: RAD agrees Appellant failed to provide sufficient credible evidence for positive claim decision

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees the Appellant failed to provide sufficient credible evidence for a positive claim decision.

propositions.text: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the RPD's decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
The appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD's decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection and dismisses the appeal.
